walkthroughs.body_html:
The People's Health c1250 to Present — a core area of GCSE History.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The People's Health c1250 to Present brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The People's Health c1250 to Present.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How did London's authorities respond to plague in 1665?
options: Infected households were shut up and marked with a red cross
The population was vaccinated against plague
A citywide network of sewers was built immediately
Antibiotics were distributed free of charge

mcqs.q: What did John Snow demonstrate in 1854?
options: That cholera was spread through contaminated water, by mapping cases around the Broad Street pump
That cholera was spread by bad smells in the air
That plague was carried by rat fleas
That smallpox could be prevented by vaccination

mcqs.q: What did the 1875 Public Health Act do?
options: Made it compulsory for councils to provide clean water, sewers and a medical officer of health
Created the National Health Service
Banned all factory work for children
Made vaccination against cholera compulsory

mcqs.q: On what principle was the NHS founded in 1948?
options: Healthcare free at the point of use, funded by taxation
Healthcare only for those with insurance
Private hospitals for all citizens
Charity hospitals run by the church

mcqs.q: Did medieval towns make no effort at public health?
options: No - although they lacked germ theory, towns passed rules about latrines, waste disposal and butchers' offal; the problem was weak enforcement, not total ignorance.
Medieval people did not care about dirt and made no public health rules at all.
Medieval towns had modern sewer systems built by the Romans for them.
The 1848 Act abolished local councils in Britain.

mcqs.q: Was miasma theory completely useless for public health?
options: Because miasma theory was wrong, the reforms it inspired achieved nothing.
It was wrong about causes, but cleaning up the smells it blamed meant removing real filth and sewage, so reforms driven by miasma still improved health.
Miasma theory was a method of vaccinating against disease.
The 1848 Act abolished local councils in Britain.

mcqs.q: Did the 1848 Public Health Act force every town to clean up?
options: No - the 1848 Act was largely permissive, letting towns set up health boards if they chose; the 1875 Act made key duties compulsory.
Medieval towns had modern sewer systems built by the Romans for them.
The 1848 Act abolished local councils in Britain.
The 1848 Public Health Act compelled all towns to build sewers and supply clean water.
